question: Alessandro controls [Angel's Tomb] and no other creatures. They cast [Mirage Phalanx]. Can they pair it with Angel's Tomb?
answer:
Yes — provided Alessandro puts the triggers on the stack in the right order.

Both abilities trigger when Mirage Phalanx enters: Mirage Phalanx's soulbond ability, and Angel's Tomb's ability ("Whenever a creature you control enters, you may have this artifact become a 3/3 white Angel artifact creature with flying until end of turn"). Since Alessandro controls both, they choose the order the two triggers go on the stack, so they can have Angel's Tomb's trigger resolve first.

- Angel's Tomb's trigger resolves: Alessandro has Angel's Tomb become a 3/3 white Angel artifact creature with flying until end of turn.
- Then the soulbond trigger resolves. Soulbond checks on resolution that both objects are creatures on the battlefield under the controller's control; if either isn't a creature at that time, neither becomes paired [702.95c]. Because Angel's Tomb is now a creature (and is unpaired), Mirage Phalanx and Angel's Tomb become paired [702.95b], and each then has the token-copying ability granted by Mirage Phalanx.

If instead the soulbond trigger resolves first, Angel's Tomb is still just a noncreature artifact at that moment, so there is no other unpaired creature and no pairing happens [702.95c]; the later Angel's Tomb trigger doesn't retroactively create a pairing. Note also that a creature can be paired with only one other creature [702.95d], and Mirage Phalanx's own text keeps them paired only for as long as Alessandro controls both.

This answer doesn't depend on the number of players at the table; nothing here involves other players' choices.

question: Addison controls [The Book of Vile Darkness], and token copies of [Eye of Vecna] and [Hand of Vecna] created by [Saheeli's Artistry]. Addison then activates The Book of Vile Darkness. What abilities will the Vecna token have?
answer:
Vecna will be a legendary 8/8 black Zombie God token with indestructible and no other abilities — it gains no triggered abilities from the exiled token copies.

Why: Saheeli's Artistry creates tokens that are copies of Eye of Vecna and Hand of Vecna, and a copy's name is a copiable value, so those tokens really are named Eye of Vecna and Hand of Vecna ([707.2], [707.2a], [111.4] — see the Spitting Image/Doomed Dissenter example). They're also artifacts you control, so they legally pay the cost of The Book of Vile Darkness's ability: "{T}, Exile The Book of Vile Darkness and artifacts you control named Eye of Vecna and Hand of Vecna."

But the ability then grants "all triggered abilities of the exiled cards," and the official ruling spells out that this ability looks at the *cards* in exile, not the permanents that were on the battlefield ([The Book of Vile Darkness ruling #2]). Token copies are not cards, so once they're exiled there are no Eye of Vecna or Hand of Vecna cards in exile for Vecna to copy abilities from. Vecna therefore enters with only the characteristics The Book of Vile Darkness itself defines: legendary, 8/8, black, Zombie God, indestructible ([111.3] — a token has no characteristics beyond those defined by the ability that created it).

Consequences of that: Vecna gets no Eye of Vecna enters-the-battlefield trigger (no card draw, no 2 life lost) even though such gained triggers would normally be copiable and would trigger ([The Book of Vile Darkness ruling #0]), and no Hand of Vecna beginning-of-combat +X/+X trigger. Contrast the normal case, where the real cards are exiled and Vecna gains the one trigger from Hand of Vecna and the two from Eye of Vecna ([The Book of Vile Darkness ruling #1]).

This answer doesn't depend on the number of players; nothing here involves opponents or defending players.

Timing note: I'm assuming the token copies were the objects exiled to pay the cost. If Addison also controlled the actual Eye of Vecna and/or Hand of Vecna cards and exiled those instead (or in addition), Vecna would gain the triggered abilities of whichever real cards ended up in exile.

question: Alfonso has 20 life and has cast a [Channel] previously this turn. Nancy casts [Word of Command], choosing [Squire] from Alfonso's hand. Can Nancy have Alfonso pay 20 life to add 20 colorless mana while casting the Squire, causing Alfonso to lose the game?
answer:
No. While Nancy controls Alfonso under Word of Command, Word of Command's own text says the controlled player "can activate mana abilities only if they're from lands that player controls and only if mana they produce is spent to activate other mana abilities of lands the player controls and/or to play that card." Channel's effect is not a mana ability of a land Alfonso controls — it's a floating effect from a resolved sorcery that lets him pay 1 life for {C} any time he could activate a mana ability — so Nancy cannot use it at all during the Word of Command play. This card-specific restriction overrides the general rule (723.5a) that a controller may otherwise freely use the controlled player's resources to pay costs.

Two further points, had the restriction not existed:
- Squire costs {1}{W}. The {W} must be white mana, which Channel's {C} can never pay; {C} is colorless specifically and only the {1} generic portion could be paid with it (202.1). So Channel mana alone can't even cast Squire.
- Under Word of Command, mana produced must be spent on that card or on other land mana abilities, so making 20 extra {C} "for nothing" isn't a legal use.

On the life question itself: paying 20 life at exactly 20 life would be legal in the abstract, since a player may pay life only if their life total is at least the payment (119.4, 118.3), and Alfonso would then be at 0 and lose the game the next time a player would receive priority (119.6, 104.3b). But per Channel ruling #0, once at 0 he could not pay any further life. That path just isn't available here because of Word of Command's mana-ability restriction.

This analysis doesn't depend on player count — Word of Command targets one opponent, so it reads the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

question: Angelica controls a [Blood Moon], a [Life and Limb], and a [Sheltered Thicket], that entered the battlefield in that order. Is the Sheltered Thicket a creature?
answer:
I can’t conclusively say yes or no with only the provided rules — the context here doesn’t include the rule that determines the order to apply multiple continuous effects in the same layer (the timestamp/continuous-effect–ordering rule), which is necessary to decide whether Blood Moon or Life and Limb “wins” here.

Why it’s undecided from the provided material:
- Sheltered Thicket is printed as a land with subtypes Mountain and Forest (see Sheltered Thicket card data and rule 305.5 and 205.1b). By the printed characteristics it is a Forest when it’s put onto the battlefield. [Sheltered Thicket, 305.5, 205.1b]
- Blood Moon’s effect (“Nonbasic lands are Mountains.”) is a continuous effect that sets a nonbasic land’s land subtype(s) to a basic land type (Mountain). Rule 305.7 says that when an effect sets a land’s subtype to one or more basic land types, the land no longer has its old land type(s), and it loses abilities generated from its rules text and old land types and gains the appropriate mana ability. So if Blood Moon’s subtype-setting effect is applied to Sheltered Thicket, Sheltered Thicket would cease to have the Forest land type. [Blood Moon, 305.7]
- Life and Limb’s effect (“All Forests and all Saprolings are 1/1 green Saproling creatures and Forest lands in addition to their other types…”) is a continuous effect that makes Forests into creatures (and also sets power/toughness). If Life and Limb’s effect is applied to Sheltered Thicket (i.e., Sheltered Thicket is considered a Forest at the time that effect applies), it becomes a 1/1 creature as part of that single effect (see 613.6 about effects that change types and set power/toughness applying to the same set of objects). [Life and Limb, 613.6]
- Which of those results actually obtains for Sheltered Thicket depends on which layer-4 subtype-setting effect is applied last (Blood Moon’s “becomes Mountain” or Life and Limb’s effect that identifies “Forests” and makes them creatures). The provided rules do not include the rule that tells us how to order multiple continuous effects that apply in the same layer (timestamp ordering among continuous effects), so we cannot determine from the supplied material whether Sheltered Thicket keeps being a Forest for the purposes of Life and Limb or has its Forest subtype removed by Blood Moon before Life and Limb would affect it.

What’s missing to answer definitively:
- The rules that specify how to order and apply multiple continuous effects in the same layer (timestamp/order-of-application rules from the comprehensive rules, e.g., the timestamp rule in the layer system). Without that, the interaction between Blood Moon’s subtype-setting effect and Life and Limb’s Forest-targeting effect is unresolved in the supplied context.

Definitions (from the provided rules):
- “Creature”: an object with the card type creature; an object that’s both a land and another card type combines the aspects of each card type (see 300.2a and 205.1b). [300.2a, 205.1b]
- “Setting a land’s subtype to a basic land type”: an effect that replaces the land’s old land type(s) with the specified basic land type(s) and causes it to lose abilities generated from its rules text and old land types (see 305.7). [305.7]

Because the decisive rule about ordering continuous effects in the same layer isn’t present in the supplied context, I must mark this answer as unresolved rather than guess which enchantment’s effect prevails.

question: Ainsley controls a [Blood Moon], a [Life and Limb], a [Cinder Glade], and a 1/1 Green Saproling Creature token, that entered the battlefield in that order. What do the Cinder Glade and Saproling look like?
answer:
Answered: no. The provided rules and rulings here don’t include the rule needed to decide which continuous effect wins when two static effects both try to change a land’s land types (i.e., the layered/timestamp tiebreak rule for continuous effects), so I can’t definitively say which final land subtype(s) Cinder Glade and the Saproling have.

What is missing (so you can get a definitive ruling): the comprehensive layer/timestamp rule (the parts of CR 613 that describe ordering of continuous effects in the same layer and how later timestamps override earlier ones). Without that rule, the two applicable authoritative rulings conflict for Cinder Glade and the Saproling and there is no way to determine which effect takes priority.

What the provided material does establish (but not the final outcome):
- Blood Moon’s ruling (#2) says that “Nonbasic lands will lose any other land types and abilities they had. They will gain the land type Mountain and gain the ability “{T}: Add {R}.” (This tells you what Blood Moon attempts to do to a nonbasic land: set its land type to Mountain, remove other land types and abilities that came from the land’s rules text or its prior land types, and give the Mountain mana ability.) [Blood Moon ruling #2; 305.7]
- Life and Limb’s card text and rulings say “All Forests and all Saprolings are 1/1 green Saproling creatures and Forest lands in addition to their other types.” In particular, Life and Limb ruling #3 says each Forest and Saproling will have the card types creature and land and the subtypes Forest and Saproling; Life and Limb ruling #1 says Saprolings enter as land creatures. That is what Life and Limb attempts to make Cinder Glade and the Saproling token into (1/1 green Saproling creature lands with subtype Forest). [Life and Limb; Life and Limb ruling #3; Life and Limb ruling #1]
- Cinder Glade’s printed characteristics are “Land — Mountain Forest” with “{T}: Add {R} or {G}.” Cinder Glade is a nonbasic land (it lacks the basic supertype). [Cinder Glade; Nonbasic Land; 111.3]
- Tokens have only the characteristics the creating effect gives them; Life and Limb’s ruling #1 says Saproling tokens enter as land creatures (so the Saproling token is affected by Life and Limb when it enters). [111.3; Life and Limb ruling #1]
- If an effect “sets a land’s subtype to one or more of the basic land types,” rule 305.7 explains that the land no longer has its old land type(s), loses abilities generated from its rules text/old land types, and gains the mana ability appropriate to the new basic land type. This is what Blood Moon’s ruling describes it doing. [305.7]

Why that still doesn’t let me give a final state here: both Blood Moon’s ruling and Life and Limb’s ruling directly describe what should apply to Cinder Glade (and to Saprolings treated as lands). They are both continuous effects that change land subtypes (layer-4 type-changing effects) and Blood Moon’s ruling tells those nonbasic lands lose their previous land types while Life and Limb tells Forests and Saprolings gain the Forest land subtype and become land creatures. To determine which effect is actually in force on Cinder Glade and the Saproling token you need the rule that orders continuous effects that apply in the same layer (the timestamp / later-effect-wins rule from the full CR 613). That ordering rule is not included in the provided context, so I can’t lawfully pick between the two outcomes here.

If you supply the missing layer/timestamp rule (the parts of CR 613 that specify how to order multiple continuous effects that apply in the same layer), I will apply it to these specific continuous effects and tell you exactly what Cinder Glade and the Saproling look like.

(Definitions of key terms used above)
- “Basic land type”: one of Plains, Island, Swamp, Mountain, Forest. An object with the land card type and a basic land type has the intrinsic ability “{T}: Add [that color]”. [305.6]
- “Nonbasic land”: any land that doesn’t have the supertype “basic.” [Nonbasic Land; 205.4c]
- “Set a land’s subtype to one or more of the basic land types”: when an effect does this, the land loses its old land type(s) and abilities from its rules text and gains the ability to tap for the mana of the new basic land type(s). [305.7]
- “Token”: a game object created by a spell or ability that has only the characteristics that the creating effect defines. [111.3]

question: Allison controls [Dralnu's Crusade] and [Leopard-Spotted Jiao]. Allison then casts [Conspiracy] naming "Goblin". What are the creature types of Leopard-Spotted Jiao and does it get +1/+1?
answer:
Leopard-Spotted Jiao becomes a Goblin and only a Goblin; it does not become a Zombie from Dralnu's Crusade and it does not get the +1/+1 from Dralnu's Crusade. 

Reasoning: Conspiracy makes “Creatures you control are the chosen type” and “Affected … creatures lose all of their other creature types,” so Leopard-Spotted Jiao’s creature type is set to Goblin (losing Beast) by Conspiracy (Conspiracy ruling #4). Applying continuous effects uses the layer system (type-changing effects are applied in layer 4) (613.1d; Type-Changing Effect). Because Dralnu's Crusade’s type-changing part is applied before Conspiracy’s (Dralnu's Crusade was already on the battlefield), Dralnu's Crusade’s set of objects it affects is determined when its layer-4 part is applied. Per the rules for multi-part effects, the set of objects an effect applies to is fixed when the effect first applies and that same set is used for its later parts in later layers (613.6). When Dralnu's Crusade’s layer-4 part is applied, Leopard-Spotted Jiao was a Beast, not a Goblin, so it was not in the set of objects Dralnu's Crusade affects; therefore Dralnu's Crusade’s later parts (making Goblins black, adding Zombie in addition to their other creature types, and giving +1/+1) do not apply to Leopard-Spotted Jiao after Conspiracy enters. (Dralnu's Crusade ruling #0 explains how Dralnu's Crusade normally affects Goblins, but it does not change the layer/timestamp interaction described above.) 

So the final result: Leopard-Spotted Jiao’s creature type(s): Goblin only. Leopard-Spotted Jiao does not get +1/+1 from Dralnu's Crusade.

question: Adriel controls [Wandering Ones] equipped with [Fleetfeather Sandals]. On Nico's turn, they enchant it with [Tightening Coils]. On Adriel's next turn, they activate Fleetfeather Sandals's equip ability, targeting Wandering Ones. After that resolves, does it have flying?
answer:
Yes. After Fleetfeather Sandals’s equip ability resolves, Wandering Ones will have flying.

Why: Tightening Coils’s text makes the enchanted creature “lose[] flying,” which is an effect that removes an ability. Fleetfeather Sandals’s static ability that says “Equipped creature has flying and haste” creates a continuous effect that grants flying when Fleetfeather Sandals becomes attached to Wandering Ones. When effects add and remove the same ability, the most recent continuous effect prevails; which effect is “most recent” is determined by timestamps (the later timestamp wins). An Aura or Equipment receives a new timestamp when it becomes attached to a creature, so Fleetfeather Sandals’s granting effect will have a later timestamp when you equip it after Tightening Coils is already attached, and therefore Wandering Ones ends up with flying. This outcome is also stated explicitly by the ruling on Tightening Coils: “If an effect gives the enchanted creature flying after Tightening Coils became attached to it, the creature will have flying.”

Assumption about timing: I’m assuming Tightening Coils was already attached to Wandering Ones on Nico’s turn and that Fleetfeather Sandals’s equip ability resolves later on Adriel’s turn. If instead Fleetfeather Sandals had been attached first and Tightening Coils became attached afterward, Tightening Coils’s later removal would make Wandering Ones lose flying.

answer:
Yes. Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth is a creature, and its creature type is Elemental (not Ferret).

Why: Vastwood Zendikon’s text makes “Enchanted land ... a 6/4 green Elemental creature” and Vastwood Zendikon’s ruling confirms “The enchanted permanent will be both a land and a creature” (so Urborg becomes a creature with creature type Elemental when Vastwood Zendikon enchants it) (Vastwood Zendikon ruling #5). Creature-type and other type changes are “type-changing effects” applied in layer 4 (613.1d, 205.1b, 205.3c). question: Allen controls [Thraben Purebloods] which is enchanted by [Kenrith's Transformation]. Thraben Purebloods then becomes enchanted by [One with the Stars]. What happens?
answer:
Direct answer: Thraben Purebloods ends up as an enchantment (no longer a creature) because One with the Stars’ later type-changing effect overwrites Kenrith's Transformation’s type-changing effect; Kenrith's creature-setting and ability-removal effects therefore don't apply while One with the Stars is winning the timestamp contest. If One with the Stars leaves, Kenrith's Transformation's effects will apply again and Thraben Purebloods will become a green Elk creature with base power/toughness 3/3 and lose other card types and (while a creature) lose abilities.

Reasoning and definitions (brief):
- Continuous effect: an effect that continuously modifies object characteristics and is applied automatically by the game (see rule 613.5 describing continuous effects applying via the layer system).
- Timestamp: when multiple continuous effects apply in the same layer or sublayer, the game uses timestamps (the time each effect was generated) to order them; a later timestamp can override an earlier one (rule 613.7 and rule 613.9).
- Both Kenrith's Transformation and One with the Stars create continuous type-changing effects that affect the enchanted permanent. When two such effects conflict in the same layer, the one with the later timestamp wins (613.7, 613.9). Because Kenrith's Transformation was already attached and then One with the Stars became attached later, One with the Stars has the later timestamp and its type-changing effect makes the enchanted permanent an enchantment and removes other card types (One with the Stars ruling #2). One with the Stars’ effect also “still has its abilities,” so it does not remove abilities.
- Kenrith's Transformation’s text and rulings show it normally overwrites colors, creature types, and sets base power/toughness and removes abilities while it makes the enchanted object a green Elk creature with base 3/3 (Kenrith's Transformation ruling #3 and ruling #2). Thus Kenrith's creature-setting and ability-removal parts do not apply to Thraben Purebloods while One with the Stars’ effect is overwriting them.
- Note about legality of attachment: multiple Auras with enchant abilities can be attached so long as the permanent meets each Aura’s enchant restriction at the time the Aura became attached (702.5c). That is why both Auras can be attached here (Kenrith's Transformation enchanted a creature, and One with the Stars can enchant a creature or an enchantment).

Practical final state while both Auras are attached: Thraben Purebloods is an enchantment (not a creature), it loses any creature card types/subtypes (One with the Stars ruling #2), it keeps supertypes, and it keeps its abilities (One with the Stars doesn’t remove abilities). If One with the Stars is removed, the later-effect status changes and Kenrith's Transformation will then make Thraben Purebloods a green Elk with base 3/3 and remove other card types and (while it is a creature) remove abilities per Kenrith's Transformation.

question: Avery manifests the top card of their library with [Soul Summons]. Then, they mutate [Trumpeting Gnarr] targeting the manifested creature. What are the characteristics of the resulting creature if Avery chooses to put the manifested creature on top?
answer:
Result: The permanent becomes a merged, face-down 2/2 colorless creature represented by the manifested card on top with Trumpeting Gnarr beneath; it is face down and has all abilities printed on Trumpeting Gnarr (including “Whenever this creature mutates, create a 3/3 green Beast creature token”).

Why: Soul Summons put the top card of Avery’s library onto the battlefield face down as a 2/2 creature (manifest) (Soul Summons). Trumpeting Gnarr, cast for its mutate cost, merges with the targeted manifested creature as it resolves and the spell’s controller chose to put the manifested card on top (702.140c; Mutating Creature Spell; 608.3d; 730.2e). A mutated (merged) permanent has all abilities of each card that represents it, while “other characteristics” (name, types, power/toughness, mana cost, color, etc.) are derived from the topmost card or token (702.140e). Because the topmost component is the manifested face-down card, the merged permanent’s other characteristics are those of a face-down manifested creature (a 2/2 face-down, which is colorless and lacks a name, printed types, printed abilities, and a mana cost as described in the face-down examples) (Soul Summons; 707.3; 708.10). Its face-down/face-up status is determined by the topmost component (110.5; 730.2e).

Putting that together: the merged permanent is face down and is a 2/2 colorless creature (the manifested card’s face-down characteristics), but it also ‘‘has all abilities of each card and token that represents it’’ so it carries Trumpeting Gnarr’s printed abilities (for example, Trumpeting Gnarr’s triggered ability that creates a 3/3 green Beast when it mutates) (702.140e; Trumpeting Gnarr). If the manifested card is later turned face up, the merged permanent’s other characteristics would then be derived from that now-face-up top component while it continues to have the abilities of both components (730.2e; 702.140e).

Jinx makes Urza's Saga become the basic land type chosen until end of turn; as a result Urza's Saga loses its old Urza land type and loses the abilities generated from its rules text (including its chapter abilities) and gains the mana ability appropriate to the chosen basic land type — because it lost all of its chapter abilities while still being a Saga, Urza's Saga is immediately sacrificed.

Timing assumption: I assume Jinx resolves and its continuous effect is applied (i.e., you choose the basic land type as part of resolution). question: Natalie controls [High Fae Trickster]. Allen activates the crew ability of [Capenna Express]. Before it resolves Natalie casts [One with the Stars] targeting Capenna Express. What happens when the crew ability resolves?
answer:
One with the Stars is put into its owner’s graveyard without entering the battlefield, and then the crew ability resolves and Capenna Express becomes an artifact creature until end of turn (crewed by High Fae Trickster if High Fae Trickster was tapped to pay the crew cost). 

Why: When One with the Stars tries to resolve as an Aura spell it checks whether its target is still legal; One with the Stars can only enchant a creature or an enchantment, and Capenna Express is currently a noncreature artifact, so the target is illegal and the Aura spell doesn’t resolve (it’s put into its owner’s graveyard instead of entering the battlefield) [608.3b, 608.2b, 303.4i]. After that, the already-activated crew ability resolves: Crew N is an activated ability that makes the Vehicle become an artifact creature until end of turn when its crew cost is paid; a creature “crews a Vehicle” when it was tapped to pay that crew cost [702.122a, 702.122b, 702.122c]. 

Definitions relied on: 
- “Crewing” / “crewed”: A Vehicle is crewed by a creature if that creature was tapped to pay the cost to activate that Vehicle’s crew ability; “Crew N” is an activated ability that taps creatures with total power N or more to make the Vehicle an artifact creature until end of turn [702.122a, 702.122b, 702.122c]. 
- “Illegal target” (for a resolving spell): A spell that specifies targets checks whether those targets are still legal as it begins to resolve; if all of its targets are illegal, the spell doesn’t resolve and is put into its owner’s graveyard (special rules apply for bestowed Auras and mutating creature spells, which don’t apply here) [608.2b, 608.3b]. 

Note on a different timing: If One with the Stars had been cast (or resolved) after Capenna Express had already become an artifact creature, One with the Stars could legally enchant Capenna Express while it was a creature; One with the Stars’s effect could then cause the enchanted Capenna Express to be an enchantment and lose other card types (see One with the Stars ruling #1) [One with the Stars ruling #1].

question: Avery enchants their [Hall] with [Unbridled Growth]. Next turn, Nickolas casts [Blood Moon]. What colors of mana can Hall tap for?
answer:
After Blood Moon resolves, Hall can tap only for {R}. 

Reasoning: Unbridled Growth grants the enchanted land the ability “{T}: Add one mana of any color” (Unbridled Growth). Blood Moon makes nonbasic lands Mountains and, per the Blood Moon ruling #2, “Nonbasic lands will lose any other land types and abilities they had. They will gain the land type Mountain and gain the ability ‘{T}: Add {R}.’” Because Hall is a nonbasic land and is affected by Blood Moon, Hall loses its other abilities (including the one granted by Unbridled Growth) and becomes a Mountain with the Mountain mana ability. The result is that Hall has only the Mountain ability “{T}: Add {R}” and so can tap for {R} only. 

Definition: To “tap [a permanent] for mana” means to activate a mana ability of that permanent that includes {T} in its activation cost (106.12b). 

Assumption/timing: This assumes Blood Moon has resolved and is governing the battlefield; if Blood Moon were later removed, Hall would regain any abilities it is supposed to have at that time (for example, an ability granted by an attached Unbridled Growth if that Aura is still attached).
